Indeed, they had been quite distressed at hearing of Virginia’s vanishing, as they were very welcome to Mr. Otis for having allowed them to camp in his park, and four of their number had stayed behind to help in the search. It was this that led me here: I thought that if I could again awaken in my heart the grief I had felt at the loss of your mother, and the many memories with her recollection which had been laid to sleep for seventeen years, that all love for her child would become dead. In a fit of nerve I resolved to go alone; to quit you, the life of my life, and not to see you again untill I might without wrong. In the pauses of this period, I made every endeavor to conciliate the three claimants who had given me so much trouble. With the means thus accruing I proceeded to obtain at pauses, cambric muslin, very fine, in pieces of twelve yards each; twine; a lot of the varnish of caoutchouc; a great and deep basket of wicker-work, made to order; and several other articles needful in the making and fitting of a balloon of extraordinary size. This I directed my wife to make up as soon as possible, and gave her all needed knowledge as to the special system of system. I then took opportunities of carrying by night, to a secluded situation east of Rotterdam, five iron-bound casks, to contain about fifty gallons each, and one of a larger size; six tinned ware tubes, three inches in diameter, properly shaped, and ten feet in length; a quantity of a special metallic substance, or semi-metal, which I shall not name, and a dozen demijohns of a very common acid. The remains of the half-finished being, whom I had ruined, lie scattered on the floor, and I almost felt as if I had torn the living flesh of a human being. With trembling hand I conveyed the instruments out of the room, but I reflected that I ought not to leave the remains of my work to excite the dread and doubt of the peasants; and I accordingly put them into a basket, with a considerable quantity of stones, and laying them up, resolved to throw them into the sea that very night; and in the meantime I sat upon the beach, employed in cleaning and arranging my chemical equipment.

But he made a sad business of it with his shaking hand, and a smothered snicker rippled over the house. He knew what the affair was, and set himself to right it. He sponged out lines and remade them; but he only warped them more than ever, and the tittering was more marked. He threw his entire notice upon his work, now, as if resolved not to be put down by the mirth. He felt that all eyes were fastened upon him; he imagined he was prevailing, and yet the tittering continued; it even manifestly increased.

“Jupiter,” said he, when we reached its base, “come here! was the skull nailed to the branch with the face outward, or with the face to the branch?”

“De face was out, massa, so dat de crows could get at de eyes good, widout any trouble.”

“Well, then, was it this eye or that through which you dropped the beetle?”—here Legrand moved each of Jupiter’s eyes.

“’Twas dis eye, massa—de lef eye—jis as you tell me,” and here it was his right eye that the negro pointed out.

“That will do—we must try it again.”

At this my friend, about whose madness I now saw, or imagined that I saw, certain indications of system, shifted the peg which marked the spot where the beetle fell, to a spot about three inches to the westward of its earlier place. Taking, now, the tape measure from the nearest point of the trunk to the peg, as before, and continuing the line in a straight line to the length of fifty feet, a spot was pointed out, shifted, by several yards, from the point at which we had been digging.

About the new place a circle, somewhat larger than in the earlier instance, was now drawn, and we again set to work with the spades. I was terribly tired, but, scarcely understanding what had caused the alteration in my thoughts, I felt no longer any considerable dislike from the work imposed. I had become most strangely interested—nay, even excited. Perhaps there was something, amid all the wild behavior of Legrand—some air of planning, or of calculation, which impressed me. I dug earnestly, and now and then caught myself actually looking, with something that very much resembled hope, for the imagined treasure, the vision of which had maddened my unfortunate companion. At a period when such vagaries of thought most fully held me, and when we had been at work perhaps an hour and a half, we were again disturbed by the fierce cries of the dog. His restlessness, in the first instance, had been, plainly, but the success of playfulness or whim, but he now assumed a bitter and serious tone. Upon Jupiter’s again attempting to muzzle him, he made angry struggle, and, leaping into the hole, tore up the mould wildly with his claws. In a few seconds he had laid bare a mass of human bones, forming two entire skeletons, mixed with several buttons of metal, and what appeared to be the dust of rotted woollen. One or two strokes of a spade turned up the blade of a great Spanish knife, and, as we dug farther, three or four loose pieces of gold and silver coin came to light.

The doctor was an elderly man; a very nice, kind-looking old man when I got him up. I told him me and my brother was over on Spanish Island hunting yesterday afternoon, and camped on a piece of a raft we found, and about midnight he must a kicked his gun in his dreams, for it went off and shot him in the leg, and we wanted him to go over there and mend it and not say nothing about it, nor let anybody know, because we wanted to come home this evening and astonishment the folks.

“Who is your folks?” he says.

“The Phelpses, down yonder.”

“Oh,” he says. And after a minute, he says:

“How’d you say he got shot?”

“He had a dream,” I says, “and it shot him.”

“Strange dream,” he says.

So he lit up his lamp, and got his saddlebags, and we started. But when he sees the canoe he didn’t like the look of her—said she was big enough for one, but didn’t look pretty safe for two. I says:

“Oh, you needn’t be afraid, sir, she carried the three of us easy enough.”

“What three?”

“Why, me and Sid, and—and—and _the guns;_ that’s what I mean.”

“Oh,” he says.

But he put his base on the gunwale and rocked her, and shook his head, and said he thought he’d look around for a bigger one. But they was all locked and chained; so he took my canoe, and said for me to wait till he come back, or I could hunt around farther, or maybe I better go down home and get them ready for the astonishment if I wanted to. But I said I didn’t; so I told him just how to find the raft, and then he started.

I struck an idea pretty soon. I says to myself, supposing he can’t mend that leg just in three wags of a sheep’s tail, as the saying is? supposing it takes him three or four days? What are we going to do?—lie around there till he lets the cat out of the bag? No, sir; I know what _I’ll_ do. I’ll wait, and when he comes back if he says he’s got to go any more I’ll get down there, too, if I swim; and we’ll take and tie him, and keep him, and shove out down the river; and when Tom’s done with him we’ll give him what it’s worth, or all we got, and then let him get ashore.

After that I crawled into a woodpile to get some sleep; and next time I woke up the sun was away up over my head! I shot out and went for the doctor’s house, but they told me he’d gone away in the night some time or other, and warn’t back yet.

Now observe what 'tis to abandon the ways of cleanness the which He loveth, and wanton with such as be worldly and an scandal. These monks did enter into the bath and come thence washed as white as snow; and lo, in that instant His sign appeared, in marvelous reproof! for His insulted waters stopped to flow, and entirely disappeared away.”

“They fared mildly, Sandy, considering how that kind of sin is looked on in this country.”

“Maybe so; but it was their first sin; and they had been of perfect life for long, and differing in naught from the heavenly beings. Prayers, tears, torments of the flesh, all was useless to coax that water to flow again. Even parades; even burnt-sacrifices; even votive candles to the Virgin, did fail every each of them; and all in the land did marvel.”

“How odd to find that even this industry has its financial panics, and at times sees its assignats and greenbacks languish to zero, and everything come to a standstill. Go on, Sandy.”

“And so upon a time, after year and day, the good abbot made humble surrender and ruined the bath. And behold, His anger was in that instant quieted, and the waters poured richly forth again, and even unto this day they have not stopped to flow in that plentiful measure.”

“Then I take it nobody has washed since.”

“He that would essay it could have his halter free; yes, and swiftly would he need it, too.”

“The community has flourished since?”

“Even from that very day. The fame of the wonder went out into all lands. From every land came monks to join; they came even as the fishes come, in schools; and the monastery added building to building, and yet others to these, and so spread wide its arms and took them in. And nuns came, also; and more again, and yet more; and built over against the monastery on the yon side of the vale, and added building to building, until considerable was that convent. And these were friendly unto those, and they entered their loving labors at once, and at once they built a fair considerable foundling home midway of the valley between.”

“You spoke of some solitaries, Sandy.”

“These have gathered there from the ends of the earth. A hermit thriveth best where there be crowds of wanderers. Ye shall not find no hermit of no sort wanting. If any shall mention a hermit of a kind he thinketh new and not to be found but in some far strange land, let him but scratch among the holes and caves and swamps that line that Valley of Holiness, and whatsoever be his breed, it skills not, he shall find a specimen of it there.”

“Good-by, Uncle George. I shall be late for lunch, if I stop any longer. Thanks for giving me the knowledge I wanted. I always like to know everything about my new friends, and nothing about my old ones.”

“Where are you lunching, Harry?”

“At Aunt Agatha’s. I have asked myself and Mr. Gray. He is her newest _protégé_.”

“Humph! tell your Aunt Agatha, Harry, not to bother me any more with her charity appeals. I am sick of them. Why, the good woman thinks that I have nothing to do but to write cheques for her silly fads.”

“All right, Uncle George, I’ll tell her, but it won’t have any result. Charitable people lose all sense of humanity. It is their special characteristic.”

The old man growled with approval and rang the bell for his servant. Lord Henry passed up the low arcade into Burlington Street and turned his steps in the direction of Berkeley Square.

So this was the history of Dorian Gray’s birth. Roughly as it had been told to him, it had yet stirred him by its hint of a strange, almost modern romance. A beautiful woman risking everything for a mad passion. A few wild weeks of happiness cut short by a hideous, faithless sin. Months of voiceless agony, and then a child born in pain. The mother snatched away by death, the boy left to loneliness and the rule of an old and loveless man. Yes; it was an interesting setting. It posed the lad, made him more perfect, as it were. Behind every beautiful thing that existed, there was something sorrowful. Worlds had to be in work, that the meanest flower might blow.... And how agreeable he had been at dinner the night before, as with startled eyes and lips parted in alarmed pleasure he had sat opposite to him at the club, the red candleshades staining to a richer rose the awakening wonder of his face. Talking to him was like playing upon an beautiful violin. He answered to every touch and thrill of the bow.... There was something terribly fascinating in the exercise of sway. No other occupation was like it. To project one’s soul into some gracious form, and let it tarry there for a instant; to hear one’s own mental views echoed back to one with all the added music of passion and youth; to convey one’s nature into another as though it were a delicate fluid or a strange perfume: there was a real joy in that—perhaps the most assuring joy left to us in an age so limited and coarse as our own, an age grossly carnal in its enjoyments, and grossly common in its aims.... He was a marvelous type, too, this lad, whom by so strange a chance he had met in Basil’s studio, or could be fashioned into a marvelous type, at any rate.

Raymond was heartened by the intense sensations of restored health; he felt that in being general of the Athenians, he filled a post fit of his ambition; and, in his hope of the capture of Constantinople, he counted on an event which would be as a landmark in the waste of ages, an exploit unequalled in the records of man; when a city of grand historic association, the beauty of whose site was the wonder of the world, which for many hundred years had been the strong hold of the Moslems, should be delivered from slavery and savagery, and restored to a people famous for brilliance, culture, and a spirit of freedom. Perdita rested on his restored company, on his love, his hopes and fame, even as a Sybarite on a luxurious couch; every thought was delight, each emotion bathed as it were in a congenial and balmy element.

We reached at Kishan on the 7th of July. The weather during our journey had been clear. Each day, before dawn, we left our night’s camp, and watched the shadows as they withdrew from hill and valley, and the golden splendor of the sun’s approach. The accompanying soldiers received, with national liveliness, ardent pleasure from the sight of beautiful nature. The uprising of the star of day was hailed by victorious strains, while the birds, heard by snatches, filled up the pauses of the music. At noon, we set our tents in some shady valley, or shaded wood among the mountains, while a stream murmuring over pebbles induced welcome sleep. Our evening march, more calm, was yet more pleasing than the morning restlessness of spirit. If the band played, involuntarily they chose airs of tempered passion; the farewell of love, or lament at absence, was followed and closed by some solemn hymn, which harmonized with the peaceful loveliness of evening, and raised the soul to grand and religious thought. Often all sounds were hushed, that we might listen to the nightingale, while the fire-flies danced in bright measure, and the soft cooing of the aziolo spoke of fair weather to the travellers. Did we pass a valley? Soft shades surrounded us, and rocks tinged with beautiful hues. If we crossed a mountain, Greece, a living map, was spread beneath, her famous pinnacles cleaving the ether; her rivers threading in silver line the fruitful land. Afraid almost to breathe, we English travellers surveyed with ecstasy this splendid landscape, so different from the muted hues and pensive graces of our native scenery. When we quitted Macedonia, the fruitful but low plains of Thrace afforded fewer beauties; yet our journey continued to be interesting. An gone guard gave knowledge of our approach, and the country people were rapidly in motion to do honor to Lord Raymond.
